name: TDengine
license: AGPL-3.0 (TDengine TSDB open source); TSDB-Enterprise, IDMP and TDengine Cloud are commercial
summary: A clustered time-series database for IoT and industrial data that gives every device its own table, grouped under “supertables” with tags.
intro: A TDengine cluster is made of dnodes, each a running `taosd` server. Inside them, mnodes keep the cluster’s metadata and health, vnodes store the data, and optional qnodes and snodes run queries and stream processing apart from storage. Applications connect through the `taosc` driver or through taosAdapter, which offers REST and WebSocket APIs and also accepts InfluxDB line protocol, OpenTSDB, StatsD, collectd and Prometheus remote write. The data model gives every device (a “data collection point”) its own table: a supertable defines the measurement columns and the tag names, such as model or location, and each subtable is one device with its own tag values. All of one table’s rows live in a single vnode, chosen by consistent hashing, so writing is a simple append. With three replicas, each vnode belongs to a Raft group that confirms a write once a majority has logged it. Data files cover time ranges set per database by `DURATION` (10 days by default), and `KEEP` (3,650 days by default) decides when they are dropped.

The open-source TDengine TSDB, under AGPL-3.0, includes clustering, Raft replication, stream processing, a cache of each table’s latest values, and Kafka-like topic subscriptions, so many IoT setups need no separate queue or cache. TDengine TSDB-Enterprise adds tiered storage including S3, encryption, backup and restore, database- and table-level access control, auditing, load balancing by splitting and merging vnodes, replication between sites, and zero-code connectors for PI System, OPC, MQTT and other sources. The company sells it together with TDengine IDMP, a layer for asset models, dashboards and AI analysis, as TDengine All-in-One: free for up to 5,000 tags since July 2026 and licensed by tag count above that, where a tag is one measured signal such as a pump’s discharge pressure. TDengine Cloud runs the same package, fully managed on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, from $970 a month.
strengths: The supertable model fits fleets of devices: a device’s table is created on its first insert, and one query covers them all with `PARTITION BY tbname` and `INTERVAL` windows
Clustering and Raft replication are in the open-source build, as they have been since August 2020
Fewer moving parts: stream processing, a latest-value cache and Kafka-like subscriptions are built in, and from 3.4.3 subscriptions can also be served over MQTT
Easy to feed: taosAdapter accepts what agents built for InfluxDB, OpenTSDB, StatsD, collectd or Prometheus already send, and Kafka source and sink connectors are open source
limits: AGPL-3.0: if you modify TDengine and let users reach it over a network, you must offer them your changed source; companies that avoid the AGPL need a commercial licence
Tiered storage and S3, encryption at rest, backups, two-replica databases and table-level access control are Enterprise only; the open build allows one or three replicas

Schema rules follow the device model: the first column must be a timestamp, and a table allows at most 4,096 columns and 128 tags, so you decide up front which supertable a source belongs to and which values are tags
Commercial pricing counts tags: above the free 5,000, a self-hosted licence starts at $12,500 a year for 7,500 tags, high availability adds 30%, and support on the free tier costs $3,375 a year
The open-source tree is built and tested mainly on Linux; macOS works for development, and Windows support is limited

snippet.title: A supertable of meters, one subtable per meter, and windowed queries
source: -- 10-day data files, kept a year, latest row of each table cached
CREATE DATABASE power KEEP 365 DURATION 10 CACHEMODEL 'last_row';
-- the template: measurement columns plus tags that describe each meter
CREATE STABLE meters (ts TIMESTAMP, current FLOAT, voltage INT, phase FLOAT)
-- each meter gets its own subtable, created on its first insert
INSERT INTO d1001 USING meters TAGS ('California.SanFrancisco', 2)
-- 10-minute averages for every meter over the last day
-- the newest reading across all meters, served from the cache

story: Jeff Tao (Tao Jianhui) worked at Motorola and 3Com in the United States, as a principal staff engineer at Motorola Mobile Devices, then returned to Beijing in 2008 and founded two companies. In 2016 he concluded that IoT data was growing into a big-data problem of its own and deserved a tool designed around it, and in May 2017 he founded TAOS Data to build one.

TDengine’s code went public on GitHub on July 12, 2019, under AGPL-3.0. Clustering followed in August 2020, the month version 2.0 was tagged, while InfluxDB kept clustering in its paid edition, a contrast TAOS Data has used in its marketing ever since. Version 3.0 in August 2022 made TDengine cloud native, with compute separated from storage and Kubernetes support, and built in caching and a message queue.

Since then the company has moved toward industrial data. TDengine IDMP adds asset models, dashboards and AI analysis on top of the database, pitched as a replacement for traditional data historians such as PI System, and in July 2026 the whole package became free for deployments of up to 5,000 tags.

choices.choice: One table per data collection point
choices.why: Each device writes its own readings in time order. Giving it a table keeps its data contiguous, so a write is a plain append and reading one device’s history is a sequential scan.

Devices of one type share a schema, and attributes such as model or location rarely change. Storing them once per subtable as tags, rather than on every row, lets one query aggregate across devices by tag.

choices.choice: Keep each table whole inside one vnode
choices.why: Consistent hashing places every table in one vnode, so a device’s data is never spread across machines, and the cluster grows by adding vnodes and dnodes.

choices.choice: Build in the cache, streams and queue
choices.why: IoT systems usually bolt a cache, a stream processor and a message queue onto the database. Version 3.0 made caching of new data and a message queue tailored for time series part of TDengine itself.
